headline: New-moon springs wake the sunset bass bite at Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk Islands
subhead: Bigger tides and a fluke exodus from the warm bays are rewriting the Central Sound playbook this week.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does in the dead heat of July — it got sticky and slow through the midday tides, then came alive right at the edges. The June full moon had worked its way out of the system, current went slack and predictable, and the water in the back bays climbed hard. Oyster Bay and Smithtown Bay have been sitting warm enough that the fluke simply left. That's not a guess — it's the same pattern we see every summer once the shallow water tips past what a flatfish wants to sit in. They don't die, they just relocate to where the current keeps things cool and moving, which this week means the channels off Middle Ground Light and the deeper cuts near Stratford Shoal.

Now the moon's swinging new, and that changes everything about how I fish the next four days. New-moon springs mean bigger tidal exchange — more water moving through the pinch points that make Central Sound what it is. Stratford Shoal, the Middle Ground rip, the gut between the Norwalk Islands — these are current funnels, and a bigger tide means more bait gets squeezed through them on a tighter schedule. The window that matters most this weekend is the PM flood stacking up against sunset. That alignment peaks Saturday through Monday, July 11-13, and it's the first evening setup like this since the June full moon faded out. When the flood tide is still building as the light goes down, bass push up onto the shoals and hold in the current seam instead of just passing through — that's your window, and it's a short one, usually 90 minutes on either side of the top of the tide.

The bass fishing itself has been honest work, not a gimme. Boats working the Stratford Shoal rip on the last few evening tides have been picking off stripers in the 24 to 34-inch range, mostly on live bunker fished on a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in 25 to 40 feet where the rip stacks up on the drop. A few guys are doing well trolling bunker spoons and umbrella rigs along the edge where the shoal falls into deeper water on the Connecticut side — that thermal break is holding bait, and the bass are sitting under it rather than chasing it on top, at least during the brighter hours. Norwalk Islands has been more of a bucktail bite: white and chartreuse 1-1.5 oz bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along the rock piles off Sheffield and Copps Islands on the last two hours of the outgoing. Nobody's filling a cooler out there, but a few keeper bass and a lot of shorts have kept rods bent, and the bigger fish have been coming right at last light, which lines up with what the tide is telling us.

Fluke have genuinely shifted. The bay water got too warm to hold them comfortably, so if you're still working the flats inside Oyster Bay or Northport, you're fishing memory, not fish. The better drifts right now are the channel edges near Middle Ground Light and the deeper humps off Six Mile Reef, 35 to 50 feet, where the incoming tide is pulling cooler water up from the main body of the Sound. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-oz bucktails, dragged dead slow, have been the most consistent producer, with a scattering of fish to 5 pounds. It's not a bay-style easy pick — you have to cover water and find where the bottom breaks, but the fish that are there are quality.

Bluefish have shown up reliably wherever there's current and bait getting squeezed — chunked bunker off Charles Island has been drawing consistent action in the 3 to 6-pound range, and topwater poppers thrown at first light off the Norwalk Islands have connected on fish blowing up on peanut bunker pushed against the rocks. Porgies are steady but unspectacular on the reef structure around Charles Island and the outer Norwalk group — bottom rigs with clam and sandworm in 20 to 35 feet, better on the last of the outgoing when the current slows enough for them to feed off bottom instead of getting pinned.

Weakfish, I have to be straight with you, are still a no-show. Water's plenty warm enough now, and every year somebody asks if this is the year they come back to the Sound in numbers. Zero solid reports again this week despite the temperature checking every box it's supposed to. Warm water is necessary but clearly not sufficient — there's something else missing from the equation, and until it shows up, I wouldn't plan a trip around them.

On the bonito front — nothing in Central Sound yet, and I don't expect it this week. The corridor's opening up to our east, spreading from Block Island toward Point Judith and Newport as that cold wall between the eastern basins finally broke down. That's still 60-plus miles from Stratford Shoal. August is when they typically push this far west, and I'll be watching bait schools off the mouth of the Housatonic and around Charles Island for the first sign of them working bunker pods from underneath — that's usually the tell before you ever see a fin.

If I had one shot this week, it's Saturday evening at Stratford Shoal, fishing the last two hours of the flood into sunset with a live bunker on a light fish-finder rig, backup rod rigged with a bucktail in case the current's moving too fast to hold bottom. Plan B is the Middle Ground fluke drift on the following morning's outgoing — cooler, cleaner water and fish that have already told us they're there.
